items.prompt: In a brand-new workspace the librarian adds a book, registers a borrower and checks the book out. Which loan id does the CLI print?
items.answer: Loan 0, as an empty workspace starts all three id watermarks at 0
distractors: Loan 1, because Values.identity(id, 1) makes each loan id begin at one
Loan 1, since id zero is held back to mean that a book has no loan
Loan 2, since the book and the borrower already took ids 0 and 1
items.explanation: LibraryData.empty() starts every watermark at 0 and ids are per record type, so book 0, borrower 0 and loan 0. The 1 in identity(id, 1) is a placeholder version. Verified with piped CLI input ("Loan 0.").

items.prompt: A book titled "Reliable systems" is lent to "Sam Reader". Both records are then renamed, and the book is returned. What does loan history show for that loan?
items.answer: Reliable systems and Sam Reader, the text accepted at checkout time
distractors: The new title and name, looked up through the loan's book and borrower ids
The new title and name, as the return rewrites the receipt with current text
Only the two ids, as the receipt keeps references and no names at all
items.explanation: checkOutBook copies b.getTitle() and person.getName() into the Loan record. Edits replace the Book and Borrower, never the Loan, and returned() keeps the text. Verified in a probe.

items.prompt: A new book (version 1) is checked out and then returned, with no other edits. What version does the current book record have now?
items.answer: 3, as checkout and return each build a replacement with the next version
distractors: 1, as only edits to the title, author or ISBN move the version on
2, as a return puts back the version the book had just before its checkout
1, since loan state lives in the receipt and not in the book record
items.explanation: Book.checkOut and Book.returnBook both construct a new Book with Values.nextVersion(version). The regression test in 04 asserts the returned book is version 3.

items.prompt: Borrower 0 has a book checked out. The librarian chooses 18 for that borrower and types YES. What happens?
items.answer: It is refused until the borrower's active loans have been returned
distractors: The borrower is archived and the active loan is closed with today's date
The borrower is archived while the book stays checked out to them
The borrower is archived and the book is made available again
items.explanation: setBorrowerActive throws "Return this borrower's active loans before archiving." when any loan for that borrower has no return date. LibraryData would also reject an active loan held by an archived borrower.

items.prompt: A book was checked out and later returned. The librarian chooses 11 for it and types DELETE. What does the CLI print?
items.answer: Change not accepted: Book has loan history. Archive it instead.
distractors: Book deleted and saved.
Change not accepted: Borrower has loan history. Archive the borrower instead.
Change not accepted: Active loan missing.
items.explanation: deleteBook rejects any book that appears in a loan, returned or not, because the retained receipt refers to it. Archival (option 17) is the retirement path.

items.prompt: Borrowers are registered with emails "", "  ", "SAM@x.org" and then "sam@x.org", in that order. Which registration is refused?
items.answer: Only the fourth, as emails are lowercased and blank ones are stored as null
distractors: The second, as two borrowers may not share the same empty email address
None of them, as the uniqueness check compares the text exactly as typed
The third and fourth, as an email with capital letters is rejected outright
items.explanation: Values.email strips, turns blank into null, and lowercases the rest. LibraryData only checks uniqueness for non-null emails, so the fourth collides with sam@x.org. Verified in a probe.

items.prompt: During a checkout, the storage replacement step throws an IOException. What does the manager expose afterwards?
items.answer: The book still available and no new receipt, as data is set after save
distractors: The book checked out with its receipt, which are written on the next save
The book checked out but no receipt, as the loan list is saved separately
An empty library until the user reloads it, as the old state was dropped
items.explanation: commit builds the candidate, calls storage.save(candidate), and only then assigns data = candidate. A throwing save skips the assignment, so accepted state is unchanged; the regression test also checks the old bytes.

items.prompt: Sessions A and B load the same workspace. A adds a book. B then registers a borrower. What happens to B?
items.answer: B is refused as the snapshot changed, and a reload lets it retry
distractors: B saves, and A's new book is lost from the file without any warning
B saves, and the two changes are merged into one snapshot
B waits on the lock until A exits, then saves on top of A's file
items.explanation: save compares the bytes B last read (baseline) with the current snapshot under the lock and throws "Library changed in another session. Reload and review before retrying." After option 15 the retry succeeds. Verified in a probe.

items.prompt: The librarian checks out a book with a due date of yesterday. Which message does the CLI print?
items.answer: Change not accepted: Due date cannot precede checkout.
distractors: Change not accepted: Due date precedes checkout.
Book checked out and saved. Loan 0. (The due date is moved to today.)
Change not accepted: Date must be within 1970..2100.
items.explanation: checkOutBook calls old.checkOut(...) before it builds the Loan, and the Book constructor throws "Due date cannot precede checkout." The Loan's own wording is never reached. Verified in a probe.

items.prompt: Books 0 and 1 exist. Book 1 has never been lent and is deleted. The librarian adds another book. Which id does it get?
items.answer: 2, as nextBookId is a stored watermark that a delete never lowers
distractors: 1, as the lowest unused id is handed out again after a delete
1, as the next id is rebuilt from the highest book still present
0, as ids restart from zero whenever a book is removed from the list
items.explanation: addBook uses data.nextBookId() and commits nextBookId + 1; deleteBook commits the same watermark. The snapshot persists it, so even a restart does not reuse 1. Verified in a probe.

items.prompt: A data directory has books.txt but no borrowers.txt and no library.snapshot. What happens at startup?
items.answer: Startup stops with exit code 1, as both legacy files are required
distractors: It starts with the books and an empty borrower list, then saves both
It starts empty and writes a fresh library.snapshot over the books
It starts with the books, and borrowers.txt is created on first save
items.explanation: load throws "Both legacy files are required; missing data is not an empty collection." main prints "Startup stopped; existing library files were not replaced." and exits 1. Verified with the CLI.

items.prompt: In menu 14 the librarian leaves the query blank and types the status Available, with a capital A. What does the CLI print?
items.answer: Change not accepted: Invalid search or status.
distractors: Search results: every active book that is not checked out
No matching books.
Search results: every book, as an unknown status means all
items.explanation: searchBooks checks status with List.of("all", "available", "out", "archived").contains(status), which is case-sensitive, and throws. The single catch in App prints "Change not accepted:" even for this read-only command.

items.front: The file store replaces its snapshot atomically, and each book and borrower carries a version. What does each of the two protect?
items.back: Atomic replacement writes one complete snapshot, so book state and loan history cannot be half-saved on disk. A record version stops an edit or checkout that was based on an outdated view of that one book or borrower.

items.front: After a version conflict, why should a future browser editor NOT fetch the latest version and retry automatically?
items.back: Because the retry would hide the overwrite decision from the user. Send the version originally read, keep the draft after a conflict, and let the user decide. A transaction alone cannot tell whether input was based on old content.

items.front: Which records does a checkout write, and which does it only read?
items.back: It writes the book (a replacement with loan fields) and appends the loan receipt. The borrower is read and must be active, but is not rewritten.

items.front: What capacity limits does the file store enforce, and why state them?
items.back: Files are bounded to 10 MiB and each collection to 10,000 records. Clear limits make a small project easy to reason about and give concrete reasons for a later SQL migration.

items.prompt: In the EF Core translation, how is a loan's receipt (book title and borrower name) modelled, and why not with a join to Books?
items.answer: As columns copied onto the loan row in the same SaveChanges; a join would show the current title
distractors: As a navigation to Books loaded with Include; copied columns would duplicate data needlessly
As a JSON column on Books holding past titles; a join on it recovers the title at loan time
As a database view over Books and Borrowers refreshed whenever either record gets renamed
items.explanation: 08-TRANSLATION line 8: the receipt becomes denormalised accepted columns on the Loans table (BookTitleAtLoan, BorrowerNameAtLoan) written in the same SaveChanges as the loan, because a join to Books would show the current title, the wrong answer for a receipt. Line 16 adds that in EF Core this is a plain column, not a navigation property, so Include, a title-history column or a view are all off the table.

items.prompt: How does the EF Core translation carry the per-record version check, and what does EF do when the version no longer matches?
items.answer: A concurrency token in the UPDATE's WHERE; zero matched rows throw DbUpdateConcurrencyException
distractors: A version read in a separate SELECT first; a mismatch makes EF retry the save with the new value
A whole-table lock taken by SaveChanges; a second writer waits until the first one commits
A trigger that bumps the version column; EF overwrites the row and logs a warning on mismatch
items.explanation: 08-TRANSLATION line 9: the per-record version becomes a row-version concurrency token ([Timestamp] byte[] RowVersion or [ConcurrencyCheck] int Version); EF issues UPDATE ... WHERE Id = @p AND Version = @expected and throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException when zero rows match. It does not pre-read and retry, lock the table, or silently overwrite.

items.prompt: How does the translation table express checkout (replace the book, append the loan) so that both rows change or neither does?
items.answer: Two tracked changes in one DbContext and one SaveChangesAsync, which is already a transaction
distractors: Two SaveChangesAsync calls inside an explicit BeginTransaction that the code must commit
A stored procedure that updates the book and inserts the loan, called through FromSqlRaw
Two DbContexts, one per table, coordinated by a distributed transaction across the two
items.explanation: 08-TRANSLATION line 10: checkout is one DbContext with two tracked changes (the book update and the loan insert) and one SaveChangesAsync(); a single SaveChanges call is already wrapped in a transaction, so either both rows change or neither does. No explicit transaction, stored procedure or second context is involved.

items.prompt: How does the translation table carry archival (instead of deletion) into EF Core, and what happens to the loans that point at an archived book?
items.answer: A nullable ArchivedAt plus a global query filter; loans keep their foreign key to the row
distractors: An IsArchived flag that a migration later turns into a real delete; loans move to history
An IsArchived column checked in each query by hand; loans have their foreign key set to null
Moving the row into an Archive table; loans are re-pointed at the copy through a trigger
items.explanation: 08-TRANSLATION line 11: archival becomes ArchivedAt DateTime? plus a global query filter HasQueryFilter(b => b.ArchivedAt == null), and loans keep their foreign key. Nothing is deleted or moved, the filter is global rather than repeated by hand, and the loans' references are left intact.

items.prompt: The translation table notes that the Java store and SQL identity columns number records differently. What does it recommend for the import path?
items.answer: Map each source id to a new key and keep the source id in a separate column
distractors: Force identity columns to start at the source's first id so every key carries over
Drop the source ids and rebuild the loans' references from book titles and names
Keep the source ids as primary keys and switch identity generation off everywhere
items.explanation: 08-TRANSLATION line 12: identity columns usually start at 1, unlike the Java store, so the import path maps source ids to new keys and stores the source id in a separate column. It neither reseeds identity to match nor discards the ids, and it does not disable identity generation.

items.prompt: The Entry Points checklist lists subtle bugs a junior might miss at the CLI. Which one concerns the messages the user sees?
items.answer: Showing a result that sounds successful even though persistence failed
distractors: Printing error messages in English while the menu labels are localized
Repeating the success message twice when the menu loop redraws itself
Hiding stack traces from users, which makes their bug reports useless
items.explanation: The Entry Points checklist (lines 64-68) lists three subtle bugs: forgetting that Scanner.nextLine() interactions are stateful and order-sensitive, adding formatting that assumes consistency storage may not guarantee, and displaying a result that sounds successful even when persistence failed. Localization, duplicated messages and hidden stack traces are not on the list.

items.prompt: Which subtle persistence bug does the review checklist warn can change how the file's final record is read?
items.answer: A trailing or missing record separator changing how the last record parses
distractors: A byte-order mark at the start of the file shifting every field over by one
A missing newline at the top of the file hiding the header from the parser
A record longer than the buffer size being split across two separate reads
items.explanation: The Persistence checklist's subtle bugs (lines 96-100) are a trailing or missing record separator changing how the last record is parsed, date parsing failures that break startup, and clean-up logic that changes the durable format. Byte-order marks, header newlines and buffer splits are not mentioned.

items.prompt: The repo has no authentication yet. If a restricted operation is added later, what does the checklist name as the junior trap, and what question exposes it?
items.answer: Treating visibility as security; ask whether the rule holds when a caller bypasses the UI
distractors: Checking roles in the service layer; ask whether the menu still hides options from guests
Logging every denied attempt; ask whether each refusal is written to the audit file
Encrypting the data files; ask whether a copied file can still be read on another machine
items.explanation: The security section (lines 169-185) says to enforce rules in the service layer, not only hide them in the UI, with one obvious enforcement point; its review question is 'if a caller bypasses the UI, does the restriction still hold', and the subtle junior bug is treating visibility as security. Service-layer checks are the recommendation, not the trap, and auditing and encryption are not discussed.

items.prompt: Which pair of subtle error-handling bugs does the review checklist list for this repo?
items.answer: Treating blank and malformed values as one, and handling missing files but not malformed ones
distractors: Retrying failed saves forever, and printing raw exceptions instead of user-facing messages
Validating input only in storage, and accepting dates outside the range the parser handles
Catching every exception at the top, and exiting with code 0 after a failed startup run
items.explanation: The Error Handling section's subtle bugs (lines 207-210) are assuming blank values and malformed values are the same thing, and handling missing files but not malformed files. Endless save retries, storage-only validation and exit codes after failed startup are not what it lists.

items.prompt: The checklist's tests section names the highest-value tests to add first. Which list is it?
items.answer: checkOutBook and returnBook success and failure paths, save-then-load round trip, due dates
distractors: Menu numbering, every prompt's wording, the process exit code and the startup banner text
Email normalisation, ISBN format checks, title length limits and borrower phone parsing
A 10,000-record load test, a two-session concurrency test and a disk-full write test
items.explanation: The tests section (lines 218-223) lists LibraryManager.checkOutBook success and failure paths, LibraryManager.returnBook success and failure paths, FileStorage.save followed by load round-trip behavior, and overdue display and due-date handling. Presentation details, field validators and load or concurrency tests are not on that list.

items.prompt: What does the 05-PRACTICE harness contract say about where the checks live and how they exercise the app?
items.answer: Outside the repo, compiling src into a temp folder each run and driving the real CLI via stdin
distractors: Inside test/, compiled once by the build tool and calling the LibraryManager methods directly
Outside the repo, using a mocked FileStorage so no data directory is ever written to disk
Inside the repo's scripts folder, replaying recorded CLI transcripts without running Java
items.explanation: 05-PRACTICE line 5: the checks are dependency-free node --test files kept outside the repo (for example ../j2-practice/); the shared helper compiles src/ into the OS temp folder on every run and then drives the real CLI through stdin. They do not live in test/, do not mock storage, and do run Java.

items.prompt: Why does the practice helper include writeSnapshot instead of creating every scenario through the CLI?
items.answer: Checkout uses today's clock and rejects a past due date, so the CLI cannot make an overdue loan
distractors: The CLI cannot add books in bulk, so the larger scenarios would take far too long to type
The CLI writes the legacy two-file format, so a snapshot file must be written by hand
LibraryData skips validation for files it did not write itself, so tests can plant bad states
items.explanation: 05-PRACTICE line 60: writeSnapshot exists because checkout always uses today's clock and the Book constructor rejects a due date before checkout, so no CLI script can create an overdue loan; the helper writes a valid LIBRARY2 file instead and LibraryData still validates it at startup. Speed and file format are not the reason, and validation is not skipped.

items.prompt: In exercise 4's table sketch, what replaces the one-active-loan-per-copy check that LibraryData enforces in code?
items.answer: A partial unique index on loans(book_id) WHERE returned_at IS NULL
distractors: A unique index on loans(book_id) covering every loan the copy ever had
A CHECK constraint on books comparing checked_out with the loan count
A trigger on loans that deletes older loans when a new one is inserted
items.explanation: 05-PRACTICE line 228: the sketched tables keep book_title and borrower_name as accepted text on each loans row, and a partial unique index on loans(book_id) WHERE returned_at IS NULL replaces the one-active-loan-per-copy check. A plain unique index would forbid a copy's second loan ever, and neither a CHECK nor a deleting trigger is proposed.

items.prompt: A librarian types a real TAB character into a book title. What happens, and what does the snapshot's Base64 encoding actually protect?
items.answer: Values.text rejects it as a control character; Base64 guards |, = and non-ASCII text
distractors: Base64 stores the TAB safely, since the encoding protects every character in a title
The TAB is replaced by a space on save; Base64 only guards the ISBN and the email
The TAB splits the row into extra fields, and the next startup refuses the snapshot
items.explanation: 05-PRACTICE line 264: a real TAB typed into a title never reaches the file, because Values.text rejects ISO control characters and the CLI answers Change not accepted; Base64 protects |, = and non-ASCII text, not control characters. The TAB is neither stored, replaced nor written into the row.

items.front: Onboarding codebase map: name the four layers, the file that owns each, and why each exists.
items.back: CLI/presentation (App.java): menu loop, Scanner input, messages and formatting; keeps user interaction apart from rules and file I/O. Domain models (Book.java, Borrower.java): the entities plus a little behavior; a stable vocabulary for what a book and a borrower are. Service (LibraryManager.java): collections, core rules, relationships, stable IDs, delegating persistence; centralizes the rules. Persistence (FileStorage.java): the data directory and reading/writing records; isolates file-format concerns from business logic.

items.front: Review checklist, Business Logic: what should a reviewer look for, and which questions should they ask?
items.back: Look for: domain rules still centralized in the service layer; stable ID generation preserved; checkout and return keeping related fields in sync; list-returning methods safe and unsurprising for callers. Ask: should this rule live in LibraryManager instead of the caller; what state must change together; what invariants should hold after success; is the state unchanged after a failure.

items.front: Review checklist, Async Code And Side Effects: why does a repo with no async framework still need the section, and what does it check?
items.back: There is no async framework or concurrency model, but side effects already exist through file I/O and time access. Look for where the code touches disk, where it depends on the current date/time, and constructors doing surprising work. Ask: does this change introduce a side effect; can this logic be tested deterministically; is there a better boundary for this time or I/O dependency.

items.front: 05-PRACTICE: what is the goal of each of exercises 0 to 4?
items.back: 0: pin baseline facts of the delivered code with the harness before changing anything. 1: an overdue projection as menu 19. 2: loan renewal as menu 20. 3: port LibraryData's aggregate rules into a validateLibrary module for a web/SQL version. 4: a dry-run importer that reads the snapshot without changing it, the first step of a SQL migration.

items.front: Onboarding reading order: the five stages and the file(s) each stage reads.
items.back: 1 Domain vocabulary: Book.java and Borrower.java (the nouns; available versus checked out). 2 Rules: LibraryManager.java (ids, checkout/return rules, related lookups). 3 Runtime flow: App.java (menu options mapped to service calls, CLI validation). 4 Persistence and failure modes: FileStorage.java. 5 Judgment: the codebase map, the review checklists and the per-file explainers.

items.front: Review checklist, Tests And Missing Coverage: which review questions does it suggest, and which subtle gaps?
items.back: Ask: what behavior would be easy to break accidentally; is there a rule or parsing path that exists in only one place and deserves a test; if a future contributor changed this, which regression would we most want caught. Subtle gaps: relying on manual testing for persistence changes, and not testing both in-memory and persisted behavior for the same feature.

items.front: 08-TRANSLATION: what does the exercise ask you to build and prove?
items.back: Model the three entities and the checkout action in EF Core on an in-memory SQLite provider, then write a test with two contexts: load the same book in both, check it out in the first, and assert that the second context's checkout is rejected as a concurrency conflict.
